title: The Morris Worm and the Limits of an Internet Built on Trust (1988)
explainer: The early internet connected a small community of research institutions that largely trusted one another, with protocols like sendmail and finger carrying no real authentication. In November 1988, a program written by Cornell graduate student Robert Tappan Morris exploited exactly that gap — weak passwords and a handful of software bugs — to self-replicate across thousands of connected machines, becoming one of the first worms to spread across the internet at real scale. The resulting disruption was severe enough that it led directly to the founding of the first computer emergency response team (CERT/CC) at Carnegie Mellon, and Morris became the first person convicted under the then-new Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. It is the clearest early proof that the client-server trust model this lesson describes isn't automatically safe just because it works.
